rows.description: The older child regresses: wants a bottle, wets again, clings. It is a bid to be held like the baby. Meet it gently and briefly without mockery; it passes when he feels secure.

rows.description: Hearing you are still my big boy while being cuddled tells the child love has not been used up. Words plus a lap, not just praise for being a good helper, keep him secure.

rows.description: Two toddlers play side by side without interacting: parallel play, normal at this age. Caregivers need not force sharing or friendship; keep enough toys and stay close.

rows.description: A toddler pushes, bites or grabs because words are missing and the wish is overwhelming. Caregiver should stop it calmly, comfort the hurt child first, name the feeling, and offer a word like mine or stop.

rows.description: The child may hug, kiss or bring a toy to another toddler with pure delight. Encourage it gently and respect when the other child pulls away, teaching early that bodies have limits.

rows.description: Being bitten or shoved by another toddler frightens the child, who cries and clings. Caregiver should comfort, check for injury, and say that was not okay, not blaming either child.

rows.description: The toddler shakes her head, throws food or says no: a first taste of choice and control, not defiance. Offer small healthy choices, keep meals calm, and do not fight over each bite.

rows.description: Forced feeding, threats or chasing with a plate make food a battle and can create fear at the table. Parents should offer, model eating together, and trust hunger to do its work.

rows.description: Eating in a lap or with family, sharing roti or rice, feels like being loved. Toddler smiles and copies. Regular shared meals build belonging; avoid screens at the table.

rows.description: The child cries when the parent leaves, wanting touch and voice to fall asleep. Consistent short routines, a lullaby and a gentle goodnight help her learn safety without abrupt abandonment.
